title: Open files: find the entry square
outcomes: Reads a position and names the open file and the half-open files, and the pawn trade that created each
Names the entry square before moving a rook onto an open file, and checks which pieces attack it
Knows a pawn can never guard a seventh-rank square, and a piece can: checks for the piece, not the pawn
Says what a defender can do (cover the entry square, contest the file, take it first) and finds the move that contests
Counts attackers and defenders on a pawn that blocks the file, and tells a protected blocker from an unprotected one
Explains the idea to a beginner with an example they can set up on a board

steps.prompt: Before any explanation: which file would you like a rook on, and which square on it could the rook land on? Do not worry about being right. You will come back to this at the end.

fields.label: A square my rook could land on, and why it might fail:

steps.text: **Today's question.** An open file is a road with no pawns on it. Roads lead somewhere, or nowhere. By the end you will look at a position and say which file is worth a rook, which square the rook will land on, who can stop it, and what each side does about it. First, learn to see the road at all.

steps.text: **A road, not a prize.** A rook on an open file with no way in still ties pieces down; it just does not win material by itself. What matters is where it can *land* in the enemy camp: its **entry square**. A common best landing [I] is the seventh rank, where the enemy pawns start and the king is boxed in. Aron Nimzowitsch's *My System* treats a file as a way to reach a point [S]. Ask: which square, and who watches it?

steps.caption: White to move. The d-file is open and no black piece attacks d7. Black's knight on e4 is also loose, so White is better for two reasons; the entry is one of them [I]. Follow the rook.

line.say: The rook lands on d7, an entry square no black piece watches. It attacks the pawns on b7 and f7.
Black pushes one attacked pawn forward. The pawn on a7 was never defended: the pawn on b7 only blocked the rook's view along the rank. Now the rook sees it.
The rook takes the pawn on a7. The landing paid off.

claims.statement: No black piece attacks d7.
From d7 the rook attacks the pawn on b7.
From d7 the rook attacks the pawn on f7.
After the pawn push, the pawn on a7 is attacked and undefended.
Landing on d7 wins at least a pawn along the engine line.
Landing on d7 is among the engine's first choices (depth 16).

steps.text: **When it usually works.** Three things usually need to hold [I]. Your rook reaches the file before the enemy contests it. The entry square is not guarded by a pawn or a minor piece. And something is waiting there: loose pawns, or a king with no room to move. If one is missing, ask what else makes up for it; a landing with tempo or a forcing follow-up can still work.

steps.text: **Why the seventh rank? [I]** Three reasons, in our reading. No enemy pawn can guard a square there, because pawns never stand on their own back rank; only pieces can. The pawns still at home can be attacked from the side. And the king is often boxed in behind them, so two rooks there can threaten mate. Edward Lasker, in *Chess Strategy*, says the side whose rooks reach the file first gets the raids on the seventh [S].

**When the landing is a trap [I].** A rook on the seventh can be cut off. If a bishop or knight attacks it, its retreat squares are covered, and the king or a pawn guards the squares beside it, the rook may be lost for a piece. Before you land, ask not only who attacks the square now but where the rook goes if it is attacked next. [H] This may cost club players more rooks than a slow arrival does. (No board yet: unchecked idea.)

**Four things a defender can try [I].** Cover the entry square with a piece. Put a rook on the file and offer a trade. Take the file first: the mirror board below is the same road seen from the other side. Or ignore the file and threaten something bigger; we show no board for that one here. [H] I suspect club players lose more games by landing on a covered square than by arriving late; we have no count. The next boards show the first two.

steps.text: **Opening the road, being first.** Files open by trades: a pawn exchange, or a capture that removes the pawn. Edward Lasker (*Chess Strategy*) advises being the side that puts rooks on the file first [S]. Znosko-Borovsky adds a question to ask before opening any line: who benefits? As a rule, opening a line tends to help the stronger side, or the side with the stronger part of the position [S]. A rule of thumb, not a law.

steps.caption: The Slav Defence, move four. Every file still holds a pawn, so no file is open. A pawn trade on d5 changes that. Follow the trade and ask which file opens.

line.say: White captures on d5 with the c-pawn. The white pawn has left the c-file.
Black recaptures with the c-pawn. Now neither side has a pawn on the c-file: it is open.

steps.text: **A pawn on the road.** Sometimes a pawn blocks the file. Nimzowitsch (*My System*) separates a *protected* blocker from an unprotected one [S]. Undermine a protected one with a pawn lever. Besiege an unprotected one: bring more attackers than it has defenders, and capture with the cheapest piece first, so you give up the least if the exchange goes on. Sacrifices to clear the file come last.

steps.caption: A pawn blocks the c-file: the pawn on c6, protected by the pawn on b7. A rook cannot take it. A pawn lever can attack it. White to move. The engine sees the position as about level either way (depth 16).

line.say: The lever attacks the blocker. Black may also decline with ...c5: the lever only gains the file if Black takes [H].
Black takes the lever pawn. The blocker has left the file: the c-file is now open for both rooks.

The c-file is half-open for White: no white pawn, one black pawn.

steps.text: **Half-open: pressure on one pawn [I].** A file where your own pawn is gone but theirs still stands is half-open for you. The rook cannot pass the blocker, but it points at it and ties defenders to it. Add attackers until they outnumber the defenders, then take.

steps.text: **The answer: not yet a landing.** The bishop and queen watch e7, and the queen, knight and rook watch e8, so a rook that jumped in would be taken. White may still put a rook on e1 to contest the file and tie pieces down; the engine counts that among its better moves (depth 16). The file here is a road to be fought for, not a landing.

**What to remember.** An open file is a road, not a prize. Find the entry square and count who watches it. Pawns never guard a seventh-rank square. Reach the file first, or contest it. A blocking pawn is protected or unprotected: treat them differently. A rook on an open file with no entry still ties pieces down. [H] Keep a list of the files you used in your own games and the squares you landed on; the pattern will teach you more than this page.

steps.prompt: Teach it back. Write four sentences for a beginner who knows how the pieces move: (1) what an open file is and what the entry square is, (2) when a rook on it works, (3) an example they could set up on a board, (4) one warning. Self-check: did you say what makes a file open, name the entry square, say when the landing fails, give an example a beginner could set up, and name one answer the defender has? Then look at your first guess and ask it again: was the e-file ready to use?

steps.text: **A model answer, to read after you wrote yours.** An open file has no pawn of either colour. The entry square is where a rook can land in the enemy camp, often on the seventh rank. It works when you arrive first, nothing covers the square, and something is waiting there. Example: a rook on d1, an empty d-file, no black piece watching d7. Warning: a bishop or knight covering the entry square can win your rook. A defender can cover the square or contest the file [I].
